beats.text: You start seeing the blocks with your eyes shut.
beats.note: Falling, turning, slotting into gaps, right at the edge of sleep. Harvard researchers put numbers on it in 2000: 17 of 27 players reported the same images.

beats.name: Robert Stickgold
beats.role: His team trained volunteers on Tetris for three days and woke them at sleep onset. The reports were eerily alike: everyone saw pieces falling, nobody saw the score, the board, or the keyboard.

beats.text: Amnesiacs saw the blocks too, with no memory of the game.
beats.note: Five patients with hippocampal damage could not recall playing. Three still saw falling pieces as they dozed. One sat down and set her fingers on the right keys, not knowing why.

beats.lead: So the images are not memories of playing
beats.text: The dream came without the memory that should carry it.
beats.note: The pictures surfaced even when the conscious record of the day was gone: evidence that sleep-onset imagery runs on a different memory system than the one that recalls events.

beats.text: The players who needed to learn the most were the ones who dreamed of it most.

beats.line: The game followed them past the edge of sleep.
